Here is a polished version that preserves the piece's distinctive voice, imagery, and emotional logic while refining its rhythm and diction:

---

You love a woman, and you wonder where she disappears to every night in some flashy taxicab, wrapped in her high heels, her corset, her wide, insolent mouth. You love that she wears her glasses only with you, how thick-lensed and cow-eyed she swears it's you alone she wants to see. You love her, and you want her ugly—if she is beautifully full, you want her gaunt; if she is perfectly lithe, you want her swollen, inflated like a cosmonaut. How could you not love her, her bouillabaisse, her orangina? When you took her to the doctor, he said, "Wow, look at that!"—and you swelled with pride, you fool, because that is what it means to be in love. Any trained eye, studying the human form, would recognize how exceptional she is, how she undoes the rest of us. But you truly love this woman—why can't anyone else see it? Everyone must grow suddenly, conveniently blind to beauty if you are to keep her. You cannot bear to lose anything, not ever. You want her flesh bare, and you want the rest of the world not blind, exactly, but paralyzed—from the eyes down. You wonder where she goes all night. If she ever leaves you, you will finally understand everything about love. If she is leaving you now, you already do.

---

I preserved the surreal juxtapositions (bouillabaisse, cosmonaut, paralysis), the second-person address, and the escalating obsessive tone, while tightening syntax and elevating word choice for a more literary, deliberate cadence. Let me know if you'd like a version that leans more minimalist or one that heightens the irony further.

outputs.L3:
I am consumed by her—by the fact of her, and by everything about her I cannot see. The hours she keeps beyond my reach, the life she leads when she is not before my eyes, have become a kind of private torment, a wound that will not close because I keep pressing upon it. I do not know where she goes when she leaves me, what she thinks when she is silent, whom she speaks to in the dark corners of her day that I have no claim upon. This ignorance does not diminish my love; it feeds it. I find myself constructing elaborate theories about her secret life, oscillating between tenderness and suspicion, imagining her in situations both innocent and damning, unable to rest in either conclusion. The not-knowing has become inseparable from the loving, as though I could not want her at all if she were fully transparent to me.

And what I want from her is a contradiction I can hardly admit to myself. I want her raised up—perfect, singular, untouchable in her beauty—and yet, in the same breath, I want her brought low, diminished, made smaller than she is, as though her very magnificence were a threat I must neutralize. I would have her worshipped by no one but me, and to secure this I find myself wishing, in some shameful corner of my heart, that she were less than she is: less lovely, less remarkable, less capable of drawing the eyes of others. It is not enough that I adore her; I want the world to have less reason to adore her too. This is not tenderness. I recognize it, even as I feel it, as something closer to a desire for ownership—an attempt to shrink the object of my devotion down to a size I alone can hold.

This possessiveness reveals itself most nakedly in small, almost absurd moments. I recall the pride that surged through me—unbidden, disproportionate—when a doctor, examining her for some minor complaint, let slip an offhand remark about her beauty. I swelled with a satisfaction that had nothing to do with her wellbeing and everything to do with my own vanity, as if his admiration were a medal pinned to my chest rather than a comment about her. I know, even as I recount this, how foolish it makes me look—how the pride of ownership dressed itself up as love, when in truth it was closer to a boy delighting in a possession that others had noticed and envied. I cannot pretend this reaction ennobles me. And yet I do not disown it; I confess it, because it is true of me.

There are moments when my desire for her turns cruel in its logic. I catch myself wishing that everyone else might go blind to her, that the world might lose the capacity to see what I see in her, so that her rare and exceptional quality would belong to me exclusively, unwitnessed and unclaimed by any other eye. It is not enough that I possess her; I want the possibility of rivalry annihilated altogether. If no one else could perceive her beauty, I reason, then I alone would hold the privilege of knowing it, and my love would be uncontested, absolute, without the anxious vigilance that now consumes me. This is, I know, a wish born of weakness rather than strength—a longing to escape the vulnerability of loving something others might also want, rather than a genuine desire for her flourishing.

And perhaps this is the deepest truth I have stumbled upon in all my confusion: that we do not truly understand what we love until it is gone. I suspect—though I resist the thought—that it will only be in her absence, in the moment she finally leaves or is taken from me, that I will grasp what she meant, what this strange, jealous, self-serving devotion actually was. Loss, I fear, is the only true teacher of love's meaning; only then, stripped of possession, stripped of the small vanities and possessive terrors that have defined my affection until now, will I finally understand—too late, perhaps—what it was that I held, and what it cost me to hold it so poorly.

# The Architecture of Her Absence

I have learned the topography of her body the way cartographers once learned coastlines—through repetition, through the patient accumulation of detail until the map became more real than the land itself. The small constellation of moles along her left shoulder blade. The place where her collarbone casts a shadow in afternoon light. The particular way her hair falls across her face when she sleeps, as though even in unconsciousness she were trying to hide something from me, some final privacy I have not yet managed to colonize.

I tell myself this is love. Perhaps it is. But I have begun to notice how my devotion resembles cartography in another sense too: the map-maker's desire is never simply to record the land but to possess it, to make it available for use, to render the wild legible. When I trace the curve of her hip with my eyes across a room, am I loving her or am I annexing her? The distinction has become impossible to locate.

She leaves the apartment sometimes after I have fallen asleep, or claims to. I wake at three, at four, and reach across the bed to find only the cooling impression where she should be. When she returns—if she returns before dawn—I pretend to still be sleeping, and lie there constructing elaborate theories: she has gone to stand beneath a streetlamp and think thoughts that do not include me. She has met someone whose face I will never see, in a bar I will never visit, and told him something true about herself that she has never told me, because I have never asked the right questions, because I have been too busy cataloging the topology of her wrists.

This is the strange mathematics of possessive love: I want to know everything about her, and yet I want no one else to know anything. I want her illuminated only within the small theater of my attention, dark to every other eye. When I imagine her walking down a street, admired by strangers, something curdles in me that has nothing to do with jealousy in its ordinary sense—it is closer to grief, as though her visibility to others were a kind of theft, as though beauty like hers should exist only for the one who has learned to see it properly, which is to say: for me.

But here is the contradiction I cannot resolve, the one that keeps me awake long after she has returned to sleep beside me, breathing evenly, giving nothing away: even as I want to hide her, I want to remake her. I notice how I have begun to suggest small changes—a different way of wearing her hair, a color she might try, a manner of speaking that might replace the one she has. I tell myself these are gifts, offerings of my attention. But they are also erasures. I am asking her to become a woman who exists only in relation to my desire, sculpted by it, responsive to it, no longer quite herself but something adjacent to herself that I have helped design.

To hide her and to transform her—these should be opposing impulses. One conceals; the other reveals through alteration. Yet in me they operate as a single motion, two hands moving toward the same impossible task: to make her entirely mine without her ever becoming someone else, to possess her utterly while somehow preserving the exact woman I first loved, before my loving began to change her.

I wonder now if this is why I cannot stop suspecting her absences. It is not that I have evidence of betrayal—I have none, only the ordinary silences of a person entitled to her own nights. But some instinct in me understands that my love, in its very structure, has already driven her toward the door. You cannot ask someone to be endlessly available and eternally unchanged, hidden from the world and yet perfectly performed for your gaze alone, without teaching them, slowly, the precise shape of the exit.

Perhaps this is why the poets always write of love through loss—not because loss is love's tragic accident, but because loss may be the only vantage from which love becomes visible at all. While she is here, I am too occupied with possessing her to understand what I am doing. It is only in the anticipation of her leaving, in these three a.m. vigils where I lie rehearsing her absence before it has even occurred, that I can see the whole architecture of my devotion: how it was always, from the first night, a kind of practice for grief. How wanting to keep her hidden was already a way of preparing for the day she would be gone, invisible to me too, indistinguishable from every other woman I do not know.

I reach for her in the dark, and she is there, warm, breathing, real. And still I cannot shake the conviction that she is already leaving—that this is not paranoia but a kind of clairvoyance, the obsessive mind's only true gift: to perceive, in the very intensity of its want, the inevitable shape of its own undoing. Perhaps this is what devotion has always been. Not a bridge toward someone, but a slow, exquisite rehearsal for the moment they are no longer there to be reached for—the last map I will ever need, drawn entirely from memory, of a country I once mistook for permanent.
outputs.L5:
# You, How, When: The Questions That Shape Us

There are moments in life when three simple words carry more weight than entire philosophies. **You**. **How**. **When**. Each one opens a door to reflection, decision, and change.

## You: The Starting Point

Everything begins with *you*. Not as an abstract concept, but as the specific person reading these words right now. Who are you when no one is watching? What do you believe when convenience isn't a factor? Self-awareness isn't a destination—it's a continuous practice of asking honest questions and sitting with uncomfortable answers.

You are the only person who will experience every moment of your own life. That makes your perspective irreplaceable, even when it feels uncertain or incomplete.

## How: The Method Matters

Once we know what we want, the next question is inevitably *how*. How do we turn intention into action? How do we build habits that outlast motivation? How do we treat others with the same patience we hope to receive?

The "how" is where most transformation actually happens. Ideas are cheap; execution is everything. It's not enough to want to be healthier, kinder, or more disciplined—you need a method, a repeatable process, small steps that compound into meaningful change.

## When: The Element of Timing

Finally, there's *when*. When is the right moment to start? When should you let go of something that no longer serves you? When do you speak up, and when do you stay silent?

Timing is often misunderstood as something external—a matter of luck or circumstance. But more often, "when" is a decision we make internally. Waiting for the "perfect moment" can become an excuse for inaction. Sometimes the answer to "when" is simply: *now*.

## Bringing It Together

These three words—**you**, **how**, **when**—aren't just questions. They're an invitation to reflect on who you are, the methods you use to grow, and the timing of your choices. Together, they form a simple but powerful framework for living with more intention.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in second person about obsessive, jealous love using strange, contradictory imagery of the body.
counterfactuals.output:
You keep her in the hollow of your wrist, where the pulse should be, and now your pulse is elsewhere—in the walls, in the neighbor's radio, in the small failing hearts of moths that beat themselves against your window all night long, jealous of the light you've become.

You have swallowed her hair and it grows now from your own scalp, a garden of her, black and glinting, and you brush it every morning with a comb made of her teeth, which she does not know she is missing, which she touches her gums for in the dark and finds only smoothness, only the smooth wrongness of a mouth that used to bite.

Your ribs have rearranged themselves into a cage for a bird that is actually her laugh, trapped mid-note, and it will not stop, and you would not let it stop even if your lungs turned to paper, even if your lungs turned to the ash of every letter you never sent her, black flakes drifting up through your throat when you try to speak of anything else.

You have eaten your own hands so that you cannot reach for other things. You have eaten your own eyes so that you cannot look at other faces, and yet you see her constantly, projected on the inside of your skull like a home movie stuck on a loop, her turning away, her turning away, her turning away, the film burning at the edges but never finishing its burn.

When she touches someone else's shoulder you feel your shoulder blossom into a wound shaped like a mouth, and the mouth says her name in a voice that is not your voice, in a voice that is the voice of every cell you've ever shed for her, skin cells like small ghosts drifting off you into rooms she's never entered, haunting furniture she'll never own.

You have grown a second stomach just to hold the jealousy, and it is always hungry, and you feed it with your own reflection, scraped off mirrors with a spoon, and still it wants more, still it presses up against your other organs until your body is mostly jealousy with a thin coating of you, like a bell that is mostly the ringing and only a little bit bronze.

At night you split down the middle like a peach and there she is, curled inside where your heart should be, sleeping, always sleeping, never looking at you, and you close yourself around her like a hand closing around water, and in the morning your palms are empty and wet and you drink what's left of her off your own skin, telling yourself it is enough, telling yourself the taste of yourself tasting like her is a kind of keeping.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem addressed to "you" about loving a woman so possessively that you want her flawed and hidden from everyone else's eyes.
counterfactuals.output:
# Only Mine

I don't want you perfect, love—
I want you scarred where I can trace
the marks that make you only mine,
a map no other hand could place.

Let your laugh stay crooked, strange,
the one that makes strangers turn away.
I'll be the only one who knows
the joke that makes you laugh that way.

Don't fix the gap between your teeth,
don't smooth the wildness from your hair.
I want the parts you'd hide from them
kept safe with me, kept only there.

I'm ashamed to say I've prayed
that beauty passes you both by—
that no one else looks twice, look thrice,
that I'm the only reason why.

Stay home. Stay small. Stay in this room
where lamplight knows you best of all.
Let the world forget your name
while I'm the one who hears you call.

This isn't love the way it should be—
I know this hunger has no grace.
I want to keep you like a secret,
folded dark, in one embrace.

Forgive me for the cage I've built
from words that sound like tenderness.
I call it love. It might be fear.
I call it need. It might be less.

But still I'd have you, flawed and hidden,
mine alone in shadowed light—
better that than shared and shining,
better wrong than lose you bright.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a literary prose poem exploring jealousy and desire, where the speaker wants to keep their lover's beauty invisible to the world.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Would Do With Your Face

I would keep you in a room without windows, love, if I could get away with such tenderness disguised as cruelty. I would tell the sun to find another subject for its worship. I would take your beauty—that terrible, generous thing you carry so carelessly into grocery stores, onto crowded trains, past strangers who do not deserve the small gift of your unguarded smile—and I would fold it like a letter never meant to be sent, and keep it pressed flat against my chest where only I could feel its shape.

Is this love or is it theft? I no longer know the difference. I only know that when the barista's eyes linger too long on the curve of your neck as you laugh at something I said, some old animal in me wakes up snarling, wants to drape you in burlap, wants to write *taken* across your collarbones in ink that never fades. I am ashamed of this wanting. I am not ashamed enough to stop it.

You are not a museum. I know this. You were not built for private viewing, and still I dream of galleries with one visitor, one guard, one masterpiece, and no one asking to buy a print.

Understand: it is not that I doubt what's mine. It's that I cannot bear the tax the world levies on beautiful things—how it borrows you a little with every glance, how strangers get to keep a version of you they invented in the half-second before you looked away. They do not know how you sound at 3 a.m., afraid of nothing and everything. They do not deserve the smallest currency of you. And yet they spend it freely, your face like loose change dropped carelessly from my own pocket.

Let me be honest in this confession booth of paper: I want to be the only witness to your unraveling. I want your beauty to exist only in the specific weather of our bed, in the particular dark that belongs to us, in no one's memory but mine. This is not devotion. This is hunger wearing devotion's coat. I know the difference and choose the hunger anyway.

Forgive me. I will let you walk into the light tomorrow. I will watch you become visible to everyone who was never meant to see you the way I do, and I will smile, and inside that smile a small war will keep on being fought, forever, in the country only jealousy maps.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental, emotionally intense piece in second person about a man obsessing over a mysterious woman who disappears at night in taxicabs.
counterfactuals.output:
# Taxi Cab Nocturne

You see her first on a Tuesday that feels like a held breath. She is standing beneath the awning of the corner bodega, rain making her into something underwater, something you want to reach through glass to touch. Her coat is the color of bruised plums. You do not know her name. You will spend months not knowing her name, and this not-knowing will become its own kind of intimacy, the way scar tissue becomes a map of what once wounded you.

She hails the cab with a hand that doesn't tremble. You notice this—the steadiness—because your own hands are shaking around your coffee cup, and you think: *how does a person move through the world with such certainty when I can't even certain my own fingers.*

The taxi swallows her. Yellow and black, a wasp-striped mouth. You watch until the taillights become two red periods at the end of a sentence you'll spend weeks trying to finish.

---

You start noticing the pattern the way you'd notice a bruise blooming under skin—slowly, then all at once, purple-yellow-green, undeniable.

She appears at dusk. Always dusk, that hour when the sky can't decide what color it wants to be, when streetlights flicker on like nervous confessions. She appears and then, within an hour, sometimes two, she folds herself into the back of a taxi and vanishes into the city's bloodstream.

You begin to time it. You are aware, distantly, the way you're aware of a fever you're choosing not to acknowledge, that this is not a normal thing to do. Normal men do not stand across the street from a bar with a notebook, marking down: *7:43 PM, red coat, Checker cab, license partially obscured.* Normal men do not feel their pulse quicken like a struck match when a stranger woman exists in their peripheral vision.

But you are not feeling normal these days. You are feeling *specific.* Filtered. Like all your blood has been rerouted toward this one tributary, this one question: *where does she go?*

---

Imagine— 

no, don't imagine, you tell yourself, and then you imagine anyway—

that she is being taken somewhere against her will. That the taxis are not taxis but something else wearing taxi-skin, doing taxi-things, and that she disappears each night into a version of the city that exists parallel to yours, folded into the same coordinates but occupying different space, like two songs playing the same note at different octaves.

You imagine she is meeting a lover. You imagine the lover has your face, your hands, your specific hunger, and this thought makes you sick with something that isn't quite jealousy because jealousy requires you to have lost something you once possessed, and you possess nothing. You possess only the shape of her leaving.

You start to imagine she is not a woman at all but a *question* the city keeps asking you, over and over, dusk after dusk: *what will you do with this feeling? what will you do with wanting something you cannot name?*

---

The bartender at the corner place—the one whose awning she stands under—starts to recognize you. "Same again?" he asks, and you nod, and he doesn't ask why you're always here at dusk, why your eyes keep drifting to the door, why you flinch when it opens and she's not the one walking through.

You've stopped eating dinner most nights. Your apartment has become a museum of half-finished things: emails, sentences, a jigsaw puzzle of Venice you started in October that's missing a piece of sky. Everything in you has become provisional, waiting-room energy, the sense that your real life is happening somewhere else, in a taxi, at dusk, with a woman whose name you don't know.

You wonder if this is what devotion feels like or if devotion and obsession are just the same fever measured by different thermometers.

---

One night—an accident, a coincidence, the universe extending a single trembling finger toward you—you're in a cab yourself when you see her getting into another one at the intersection.

Your mouth opens. "Follow that cab," you say, and it feels absurd, cinematic, like you've stepped into a film about a man like you rather than being a man, actually, really, viscerally alive inside your own ribcage.

The driver glances back. "You serious?"

"Please."

You chase her through the city's veins—down streets slicked with the day's last light, past the river throwing back the skyline like a held mirror, past a woman walking a dog that stops to stare at nothing, past your own reflection in a darkened storefront window, looking startled, looking *hungry.*

The cab ahead stops outside a building you don't recognize. Brick, unremarkable, the kind of building that could be an office or an apartment or a therapist's practice or nothing at all, just brick pretending to be significant because you've decided it is.

She gets out. She doesn't look back—why would she, she doesn't know you exist, has never known you exist, you are a stranger to her in the most complete sense of the word—

and she goes inside.

You sit in the idling cab, meter ticking upward, and you feel something collapse in you, quiet as a folding chair.

---

Here is what you understand, finally, sitting there with your hands shaking again, the city breathing its exhaust around you:

She was never a mystery. She was a woman going to visit her mother, or attending a support group, or seeing a therapist, or meeting a friend for dinner, or doing any one of ten thousand mundane, human things that mundane, human people do at dusk in this city.

The mystery was never her. 

The mystery was you—the shape of your want, the way you'd built a cathedral out of a stranger's coat color and the particular slant of rain. You had needed her to be unknowable because your own life had become so entirely, exhaustingly known. Because obsession is easier than grief. Because wanting someone from a distance means you never have to survive the terror of being wanted back, or not being wanted, or being *known,* actually known, in all your shaking-handed, half-eaten, unfinished-puzzle ordinariness.

You pay the driver. You get out into the deepening dark.

You do not go into the building. 

You walk home instead, past the bar, past the awning, past all the places where you built her out of nothing, and you let her go the way you should have let her go from the very first Tuesday—

gently, 

and completely, 

into the mouth of a taxicab that was only ever a taxicab, 

taking a woman only ever herself, 

toward a life that was never, not once, about you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic monologue about paranoid love—wanting someone to be less beautiful so no one else can see what you see.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I'd Take From You

I want to steal the light from your face
just enough that strangers stop turning
when you walk into rooms I thought were only mine.

Isn't that terrible? Say it's terrible.
I'll say it again anyway—

I want your beauty rationed like wartime sugar,
want to hoard the way your laugh unstitches itself
into something helpless and real,
want to be the only witness
to the specific gold your eyes turn
in this particular slant of October light.

Everyone else can have the version of you
that photographs well.
I want the one who talks in her sleep,
who doesn't know she's beautiful
until I tell her, badly, at 2 AM,
like it's a confession instead of a compliment.

I know what this is.
I know love isn't supposed to want you smaller,
dimmer, less than what you are—
that's not love, that's just fear
wearing love's coat, standing at the door,
asking to be let in anyway.

But god, when he looked at you today,
when I watched his eyes do the math
that mine did months ago—

I wanted to reach into the air
and take back some invisible percentage,
redistribute it into shadow,
so that what's left is still stunning
but only to someone
who already knows the whole equation,

who has memorized you
in bad lighting,
in silence,
in the ordinary Tuesdays
that don't make anyone else look twice.

I don't want you diminished.
I want to be the only one
with the right eyes to see you fully—

which is just another way
of saying I don't trust
that anyone could look
and *not* want to keep you,

which is just another way
of saying I don't trust
myself to be enough,
even standing this close
to everything I'm afraid to lose.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
